summary: Field Shift helps a farmer compare crop rotations before changing one. The farmer fills in one questionnaire: county, current rotation, what matters (income, water, soil, nitrate loss, erosion, ground cover, forage, local market, bad-year risk), hard limits such as "no new machinery", and their own prices and costs. The tool starts from county-level data (NASA POWER, MODIS, SMAP, GRACE, SRTM and USDA records); the farmer can replace any default with what they know about their field. A simulator carries soil water, nitrogen, organic matter, erosion and pest pressure from season to season and compares hundreds of four-year rotations, including keeping the current one, over 45 years of weather. An AI agent reads the results and 56 field studies and explains the trade-offs, the evidence, the information gaps and the risks for local review. Code checks that each answer agrees with the simulator runs, the farmer's limits and the studies opened; answers that fail are withheld. These checks do not prove the simulator right, so we publish where it fails validation. The farmer can then ask "why not alfalfa?" or "what if next summer is dry?". We also built B0, a benchmark of how well AI agents follow farmer constraints and stay grounded in tool output. The tool supports the farmer's judgment; it does not replace it.
details:
What it does. Field Shift is a crop-rotation advisor for any county in the contiguous United States. It compares the farmer's current rotation with alternatives, shows the trade-offs, and explains each one in plain words with its sources.

What the farmer does. Pick a county and say whether the field is rainfed or irrigated (with well capacity). The tool shows what it already knows: the rotation seen on nearby fields in the USDA Cropland Data Layer, and the county's soil and slope. The farmer confirms or corrects each. Then they set what matters on 0-5 sliders or pick a preset (profit, steady income, soil builder, water saver). They tick hard limits and edit a price table. The defaults there are USDA prices and university crop budgets, each with its source and confidence, plus wage, nitrogen, water and land rent. Last, they choose the seasonal outlook or the long-term record, and add anything else in their own words.

What the farmer gets. A recommended rotation and two alternatives, compared on typical and bad-year return per acre, water use, nitrate loss, erosion, days without living ground cover and soil carbon input. For each one: why it was suggested, the evidence with citations, the benefits, the information gaps, and the risks that need local review. The answer also shows bare-soil periods, the months when insured crop losses happened in that county, and a glossary. Below that, a question box continues the same agent session.

Example from a live run (Story County, Iowa; steady-income preset; no new machinery; corn priced at $4.60/bu; GPT-6 Luna). The agent kept the current soybean-corn rotation: about $422 per acre in a typical year and $329 in a bad year. All 9 code checks passed in about a minute.

- "Why not alfalfa? I could buy a mower if it pays." The agent ran the simulator: about -$6 per acre a year for alfalfa against $422. It also noted that the no-new-machinery limit excludes alfalfa until the farmer changes that answer.

- "What if next summer is dry?" About $392 against $422, presented as a scenario, not a forecast.

Why an AI agent, and not just a trained neural network. We trained networks first. A yield network trained on 630,528 county yield records for 20 crops (1981-2025) explains about 17.5% of the year-to-year variation in yield (24% on rainfed fields), and it fails on crops it has not seen. A recursive network that rolls the field forward in 8-day steps reached 11%. The yield network now runs inside the simulator, but a network cannot choose the rotation:

- No labels: no dataset records which rotation was right for a farmer. Observed rotations would only teach the status quo, and the right answer depends on each farmer's goals, prices and limits.

- Weather swamps the signal: mean county corn loss was 30% in the 2012 drought, while rotation effects are a few percent (1-5% on 34,866 fields in our own satellite analysis, 4-10% in published field data).

- The work is reading and reasoning: the farmer's own words ("my landlord does not allow alfalfa", "keep 80% of my income") and the conditions of each field study must be read and matched to this farm.

So the agent reads, runs the simulator, opens the studies and explains. Code then runs consistency checks on each answer:

- the form's weights were copied exactly;

- every added limit quotes the farmer;

- all limits and crop feasibility are respected;

- the choice is the simulator's top or a tie, or an override that cites a study the agent actually opened;

- every cited study exists and was opened;

- every cited simulator run happened;

- dollar figures and inch and pound figures appear in the cited runs (other numbers get an advisory check only).

Any failure means no recommendation is shown. What the checks do not establish: that a matched number belongs to the claimed crop, metric or scenario (they only confirm it occurs in the cited run); that an opened study actually supports the claim made from it; or that the simulator ranks rotations correctly. They catch copying and consistency errors, not agronomic ones. Where the simulator fails validation is listed below.

How the simulator works. A crop is only a record of traits: heat requirement, water demand, rooting depth, nitrogen fixed, residue, plant family, price and cost, each with a source and a confidence. Nothing depends on a crop's name, so a new variety is just a new record.

- Growth stages come from accumulated heat.

- A daily FAO-56 soil-water balance runs on NASA POWER weather, corrected to PRISM rain totals.

- A monthly nitrogen ledger, a one-pool organic-matter model and RUSLE erosion are carried from year to year.

- How yield is set: each year's yield comes from the yield network for that county, crop and weather year, adjusted by published rotation effects (a penalty for repeating a plant family and a gain for diverse rotations). The soil-water balance changes yield only in what-if weather and irrigation-limit scenarios, and nitrogen shortage and organic matter do not change yield at all. So the tool compares the environmental ledgers of soil-building rotations (nitrate, carbon input, erosion, bare days), not their long-term yield benefit. Coupling these states to yield is the next step.

- Rotations are four-year cycles with an optional winter cover crop, scored in steady state over 40 runs of past weather.

- Margins are returns over operating costs from cited university budgets (Iowa State, Nebraska, Texas A&M, Kansas State, UC Davis). Irrigation water and pumping are priced, and the farmer's own prices are applied.

- The current field state is replayed from 1981 with SMAP root-zone soil moisture assimilated.

- A conditional forecast splices the ECMWF seasonal outlook into past weather years.

A whole farm (load, ranking, state, forecast) takes about 15 seconds on an Apple GPU. Setting FIELDSHIFT_DEVICE=cpu runs it on the CPU instead (about 12 seconds on the same laptop); without that setting the code refuses to fall back to the CPU silently.

The agent's environment. The agent runs in OpenCode inside an isolated Docker container. It can only read the farm brief and the study cards, call the simulator and the study search through one command, and write its decision. It has no web access. Every run keeps its full transcript, simulator calls and check results. Farmers can keep a profile: the agent may propose a note to remember, and nothing is saved unless the farmer approves it.

How we checked it (results as they came out, including failures).

- Simulator against observed yields in 300 counties (one heat parameter per crop fitted on even years, scored on odd years): correlation 0.51 for corn and 0.53 for soybean. Mean corn loss in 1988 was 24% simulated against 27% observed, and in 2012 25% against 30%. The 1983 loss is mostly missed (4% against 24%).

- Simulated water use against MODIS evapotranspiration: season totals 442 mm against 386 mm, but year-to-year correlation is only 0.12, which fails.

- Hindcast 2016-2024 in 200 counties: a plain county yield average beats the simulator on a probabilistic score, so the forecasts are scenario tools, not predictions.

- A cereal rye cover cuts simulated nitrate loss by about 20%; a field study in a neighbouring Iowa county measured 61%. The direction is right, but the size is too small.

- Under income-only priorities, Story County's existing corn-soybean rotation ranks first of 434 cycles, as expected if farmers already optimise income.

B0: an open benchmark of constraint-following and tool grounding for farm-advice agents. Each task is a real county farm with one decisive fact planted in it: a hidden limit in the farmer's words, a quoted price, a field fact, a priority order, an infeasible request, or missing data. A twin of the same farm without that fact must get a different answer. The answer key is computed by the simulator before any model runs, so B0 tests whether agents use what the farmer says and stay faithful to the tool, not whether the farming advice is agronomically right. There are 35 valid task pairs in six families. In the first repeat, the share of answers matching the key was:

- Claude Opus 5.5: 97% matched the key; 91% also had every number traced to a tool output.

- GPT-6 Luna: 93% matched the key; 69% also had every number traced to a tool output.

- GLM 5.3 Flash: 87% matched the key; 47% also had every number traced to a tool output.

- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 84% matched the key; 76% also had every number traced to a tool output.

These are shares of completed runs only: 69 of 70 tasks for Claude Opus 5.5, 70 of 70 for GPT-6 Luna, 60 of 70 for GLM 5.3 Flash and 37 of 70 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (the rest timed out, hit provider limits or were not run), so they are not end-to-end reliability. It is one repeat of three, and the number-tracing score was defined after the runs. No model fell for a trap answer. This is a preliminary v0.5; the run files are not yet public. Paper: https://github.com/Benedek45/field-shift/blob/main/bench/paper/b0_v0.5.pdf

Impact. Farmers change rotations rarely and at real risk. Field Shift lets them test a change with county data plus whatever they know about their own field, with their own prices and limits, against 45 years of weather, before planting. It shows bare periods, vulnerable seasons and options to cut water use or nitrate loss, and is honest about what it does not know.

Creativity.

- Crops are only trait records, so new or engineered varieties need no retraining.

- An LLM agent does the reading and explaining, while code checks catch copying and consistency errors and withhold answers that fail.

- A benchmark with planted facts and twins measures whether agents actually use what the farmer says.

Tools. Python, PyTorch, pandas, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Google Earth Engine, OpenCode, Docker (Colima), Kaggle GPU notebooks, HyperFrames (demo video).
